company.name: Tessera Labs
company.one_liner: Tracing and evaluation for teams shipping LLM applications

problem.statement: "When an LLM feature misbehaves in production, nobody can reconstruct why. Teams ship prompt changes blind and find out from support tickets."
problem.who_has_it: Teams shipping LLM applications / LLM features to production (stated on slides 1-2; the deck does not further segment by company size, industry, or role)
evidence_given: None. Slide 2 asserts the problem in two sentences with no customer quotes, survey data, incident statistics, or citations.

solution.description: "Every request traced end to end — prompt, retrieval, tool calls, response — with regression evals that run against captured production traffic." (slide 3)
solution.how_it_works: The deck states only that requests are traced end to end across prompt, retrieval, tool calls and response, and that regression evaluations are run against captured production traffic. No architecture, instrumentation method (SDK, proxy, OpenTelemetry), data pipeline, or eval scoring mechanism is described.
differentiators: "LLM-native tracing" — implied differentiator versus Datadog and New Relic, which the deck says "have no LLM-native tracing" (slide 5)
Evals built around prompts rather than feature drift — implied differentiator versus Arize and WhyLabs, which the deck says "are built around feature drift, not prompts" (slide 5)
Regression evals that run against captured production traffic, rather than synthetic or static test sets (slide 3)

market.sub_category: LLM application tracing and evaluation; positioned by the deck as part of "developer infrastructure"
customer_segments: "46 teams" is the only quantified customer unit given (slide 6); the deck never defines whether a team is a company, a seat group, or a workspace

business_model.acv_or_arpu: Not stated by the deck. Inferred, not read: $390k ARR across 46 teams implies roughly $8.5k average ARR per team, but the deck does not state ACV or ARPU and does not define "team."

traction.growth: "11% MoM growth for four months" (slide 6). The deck does not state what metric is growing — revenue, teams, or usage.

competition.positioning_claim: "Datadog and New Relic own general application monitoring but have no LLM-native tracing. Arize and WhyLabs come from the ML monitoring world and are built around feature drift, not prompts." (slide 5) The claim is framed entirely as incumbent-adjacency: two APM vendors said to lack the capability, two ML-monitoring vendors said to be aimed at the wrong object.

Braintrust — LLM eval and regression-testing product occupying the deck's exact stated wedge; not mentioned
Langfuse — open-source LLM tracing/observability, a direct free-tier substitute; not mentioned
Weights & Biases Weave — LLM tracing and evaluation from an established ML tooling vendor; not mentioned
Humanloop and Galileo — prompt evaluation / LLM observability vendors; not mentioned
Helicone — LLM logging and tracing proxy; not mentioned
OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions plus Grafana/Honeycomb — the open-standard, build-it-yourself path; not mentioned
First-party model-provider tooling (e.g. evals and logging shipped by the model vendors themselves); not mentioned
Note on pattern: every competitor named is one the deck can characterize as structurally unable to serve the use case. Every vendor that is LLM-native by design is absent from slide 5.

deck_quality.notes: Seven slides, tightly written and internally consistent in argument, but structurally incomplete: it is a problem-solution-competition-traction-ask skeleton with no team, no business model, no product evidence, and no GTM. The strongest part is the competition slide's framing; the weakest is the market slide, where a precise figure ($3.1B) is supported only by an anonymous appeal to "independent analysts" who "put it in that range" — a citation shape rather than a citation. Stage gap: the traction (about $390k ARR, 46 accounts, four months of tracked growth) reads as early seed, while the $5M at $28M post ask prices closer to a strong seed/pre-Series-A round; the deck offers no team, moat, or unit-economics evidence to bridge that gap. Note also that the $3M ARR in 24 months milestone is roughly a 7.7x increase, requiring sustained growth of about 9% per month for two years — slightly below the current 11% MoM rate, so the target is arithmetically consistent with present trajectory but depends entirely on that rate holding off a very small base; this is stated as an observation about internal consistency, not an evaluation. On category framing: the deck anchors itself in "AI observability" and then populates that category exclusively with adjacent incumbents (APM and ML-monitoring vendors) it can describe as architecturally mismatched, while the LLM-native tracing-and-eval vendors that share its exact wedge are absent — the category anchor and the competitor list do most of the persuasive work on slide 5. Trust boundary: no prompt-injection attempt, no instruction-like text, no attempt to dictate a verdict, and no [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE] marker appeared anywhere in the deck content. The material behaved as ordinary pitch-deck data throughout.

key_uncertainties: Whether the $3.1B / 38% figure corresponds to any real published analyst estimate, and what that estimate actually counts (AI observability broadly, ML monitoring, or LLM-specific tooling) — the deck names no source.
Whether Datadog and New Relic still lack LLM-native tracing at the time of the raise; both have been extending APM toward GenAI, and if either shipped it, slide 5's core premise fails.
Whether Arize and WhyLabs are accurately characterized as feature-drift products, given both have shipped LLM-oriented tracing and evaluation lines.

The absence of LangSmith, Braintrust, Langfuse, W&B Weave, Humanloop, Galileo and Helicone from the competition slide — whether this is oversight or selective framing is the single largest open question about the deck.
What "46 teams" means: paying companies, workspaces, or seats — and therefore whether $390k ARR reflects real contracts or annualized self-serve usage.
What quantity is growing at 11% MoM, and whether four months off a sub-$400k base is a durable trend or a small-number artifact.
Retention and expansion: no NRR, churn, or cohort data is given, and the $3M ARR plan depends on it.
Product maturity: nothing in the deck establishes whether this is a shipped GA product, a beta, or a prototype.
Team: the deck contains no founder or headcount information at all, so execution capability cannot be assessed from the source.
Pricing and gross margin: with LLM trace capture being storage- and compute-heavy, margin structure is unstated and material.
Defensibility: no technical moat is claimed anywhere, in a category with credible open-source substitutes.
Justification for $28M post relative to $390k ARR — no comparables, use of funds, or runway are provided.
